summary:
Antioquia department stands under Colombia's national legal framework. The department-specific signal in this inventory is dominated by lethal violence: on 5 April 2025 a video circulated showing 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja beaten and thrown into a waterway in Bello, Antioquia, in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. President Gustavo Petro ordered an investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025, after two gay men earlier in the year.

Two further Antioquia-specific findings bear on what a trans visitor may face. A clinic reportedly declined to treat Millerey as an emergency "because she didn't get shot," raising a documented concern about care access for a trans person presenting after assault. Bello's city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name, indicating that municipal authorities may handle a trans person's identity inconsistently.

National context reported alongside these Antioquia events, which the parent record carries in full, recorded 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 and 41 transgender women killed in 2023 with eight more between February and April 2024. No Antioquia-specific source in this inventory covers those national tallies or the "social cleansing" flyer campaigns run by armed groups in Caquetá, a separate department where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement.
tangentialFactors:
The Bello killing took place in a municipality within the Medellín metropolitan area, and the onlooker filming reflects a documented pattern of violence being recorded and circulated. Reporting on the case placed it within a national pattern of rising killings of trans Colombians in 2025.

The Guardian's July 2024 reporting on Caquetá, a different department, describes armed groups distributing street and WhatsApp flyers announcing a "social cleansing" targeting "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes," with trans women fleeing after death threats. That reporting also supplies the national 2023 and early-2024 kill tallies. Neither the Caquetá flyer campaigns nor those national figures are sourced to Antioquia specifically, and no Antioquia-specific source in this inventory documents armed-group threat campaigns within the department.
localsOnly:
Residents of Antioquia share the national legal framework for changing the sex marker on identification by notarial declaration, and the national identification markers for trans and non-binary people introduced in November 2025. The parent record carries those provisions.

Municipal practice in Bello drew criticism for using Sara Millerey González Borja's pre-transition name after her killing, a department-specific instance of official handling of a trans person's identity. No Antioquia-specific source in this inventory addresses resident-facing matters such as local health-service protocols for trans patients, departmental education or employment protections, or the operation of the national protection machinery for at-risk LGBTI people within the department.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the investigation President Petro ordered into the Bello killing has produced charges or convictions is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved. The identity and disposition of the onlookers who filmed the assault, and whether any were prosecuted, are likewise not sourced.

The claim that a clinic refused emergency treatment to Millerey is attributed in the reporting as "reportedly"; the facility is not named and the account is not independently corroborated in this inventory. Whether that refusal reflected a policy, an individual decision, or a misreading of triage protocol is unresolved.

No Antioquia-specific source in this inventory covers the national 2023-2024 kill tallies, the Caquetá flyer campaigns, or the department's own per-capita share of national anti-trans killings; any ranking of Antioquia by raw counts would lack a denominator here. Local enforcement of the national gender-marker process, access to trans-specific healthcare within the department, and the availability of shelters or protection measures for at-risk trans residents in Antioquia are not sourced.
